workedExample.weakAnswer: Run all four at once: the park will not bring more teenagers; even if it does, it is a handful of skaters; actually the park pulls teens off the surrounding streets; and honestly, more teenagers around would be good for the neighborhood anyway. Four answers beat one — we win this argument four different ways.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Label each answer by what it does to the chain before running any of them. “The regional skate park two towns over already absorbs the skaters — this park will not add teenagers to the neighborhood” denies the action-outcome connection: a no-link, defense. “Teens already hang around the pharmacy and the bank steps; a park gathers them into one supervised corner, so the streets see fewer roaming teens” reverses the connection: a link turn, offense. “Even if the park draws a few more teens, a dozen kids on a Saturday is not the noise and trouble they describe” shrinks the endpoint: impact defense. “More teenagers around would be a benefit, not a harm — young people out in the open, known to their neighbors, make a street feel alive” reverses the value of the very outcome they forecast: an impact turn, offense. Now test the pair of reversals. Both are about the same outcome — teenagers around this neighborhood, now, on these streets — and granted together they say the park removes something we have just called good. They collide, so choose one story: run the link turn and leave the more-teens-is-good thought unsaid, or run the impact turn and drop the claim that the park thins the streets.
workedExample.whyItWorks: Two things happen here that the weak answer skips. Each response is classified by which part it touches and what happens to that part — disappear, shrink, or reverse — which is what makes the no-link defense, the shrink defense, and the two reversals offense. Then the reversals are tested against each other on the outcome itself. It is the same outcome in both, so the test applies at all; what convicts them is that granting both makes our own park the thing that removes the good we have just named. Had the link turn been about teenagers on the surrounding streets and the impact turn about teenagers inside a fenced park, they would have been two different outcomes and both could have stood. Counting reversals would never have told you either way.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Your team proposes moving the school start time to 9 a.m. The opponent answers: “A later start will push practices into the evening, and evening practices keep athletes out past dark.” Which part of what they said is the link?
choices: The school would move its start time from eight in the morning to nine
A later start will push the school’s sports practices into the evening
Evening practices keep the school’s athletes out on the roads past dark
The school day would end an hour later than the families are all used to
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: A later start will push the school’s sports practices into the evening
guidedQuestion.hint: The link is the causal claim that the action produces an outcome.
guidedQuestion.explanation: The action is moving the start time; the impact is the harm of being out past dark. The link is the middle claim that the action produces the outcome — a later start pushing practices into the evening. The fourth is a real consequence of the action, but they never said it, so it is no part of their chain.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Your school proposes compost bins in the cafeteria. The opponent argues: “Compost bins will attract pests, and pests in a cafeteria are a health hazard.” You answer: “These are sealed bins emptied daily — schools running this exact system report no change in pest sightings.” If your answer succeeds, what has it done?
choices: A link turn: the pest problem they raised now gives the judge a reason to want bins
A no-link: the outcome they predicted never arrives at all, so nothing counts for you
An impact turn: the pests arrive, and their presence is defended as good for the school
Impact defense: the pests still arrive but matter far less to a cafeteria than claimed
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: A no-link: the outcome they predicted never arrives at all, so nothing counts for you
practiceQuestions.hint: Ask what is true if it succeeds: has the outcome vanished, or moved the other way?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The answer says the outcome does not arrive at all. That is a no-link, and it is defense: their argument goes, and nothing new counts for your side. A link turn would have to claim the bins lower pest numbers below what the cafeteria has now, which is not what was said, and neither impact answer applies to an outcome the answer denies.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The town proposes lighting the river trail at night. The opponent argues: “Lighting will draw crowds of evening visitors, and nightly crowds are the last thing this quiet neighborhood needs.” You answer: “They are right that the visitors will come, and that is the good news — a trail with people on it every evening is a trail residents feel safe walking.” Which move is that?
choices: An impact defense: the crowds still arrive, and the answer cuts how much that presence would cost
An impact turn: the crowds still arrive, and the answer makes their arrival the case for the plan
A link turn: fewer crowds arrive, and the answer says the unlit trail draws more of them now
A no-link: the crowds do not arrive, and the answer says lighting is not what brings them out
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: An impact turn: the crowds still arrive, and the answer makes their arrival the case for the plan
practiceQuestions.hint: Shrinking leaves the outcome bad. Reversing makes it good.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The answer never says the crowds will be smaller or quieter. It grants that they arrive and argues their arrival is a benefit, which reverses the value of the endpoint: an impact turn, and offense. Impact defense would leave the crowds a nuisance and shrink it; the two link answers describe things this answer never claims.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Your side proposes homework-free weekends. The opponent argues: “Without weekend homework students will forget material by Monday, and that forgetting forces teachers to spend class time reteaching.” Which response is an impact turn?
choices: Students remember more after real rest, so Monday classes would start sharper than now
Two days of forgetting needs a five-minute Monday warm-up, a small cost to the week
Those extra class reviews are how knowledge sticks, so the learning would end up deeper
Their forgetting claim rests on research about the long summer holiday, not two days away
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Those extra class reviews are how knowledge sticks, so the learning would end up deeper
practiceQuestions.hint: An impact turn grants the outcome and reverses what it is worth.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Their endpoint is the reteaching, called a cost. The reteaching answer grants it happens and argues it is a benefit: an impact turn. The remembering answer reverses the connection instead, so it is a link turn. The warm-up answer shrinks the cost and stays defense, and the summer-holiday answer goes after their evidence, which is an indict and also defense.

masteryCheck.prompt: Your side proposes a Saturday farmers market in the school lot. The opponent argues: “A market draws outsiders onto campus, and outsiders on school grounds are a safety risk.” You give two answers: a staffed market means fewer unsupervised strangers drifting through the lot than it gets on an empty Saturday now; and the stallholders and shoppers a market brings are good for the school, because they buy from student fundraisers. Do these two answers collide?
choices: Yes, because two reversals aimed at one opposing argument compose into a double turn
No, because the first answer names the drifters and the second the paying shoppers
Yes, because granting both would mean the market removes the very shoppers we called good
No, because a debater may give the judge as many answers as the speech time allows
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: No, because the first answer names the drifters and the second the paying shoppers
masteryCheck.hint: Name the outcome each answer is about before you count anything.
masteryCheck.explanation: Run the test. The first answer is about unsupervised strangers drifting through the lot; the second is about stallholders and shoppers. Different people, so granting both leaves the opponent nothing: the market removes the drifters and brings the shoppers, and nothing we said takes away the good we named. Two reversals do not collide by being two, and the number of answers you may give is a separate question from whether granting both would hand the opponent a reason against you.

masteryCheck.prompt: You are defending a fenced dog park. The opponent argues: “a dog park brings more dogs into the neighborhood, and more dogs mean more noise.” You have drafted two responses: the fenced park pulls the neighborhood’s dogs off the sidewalks into one enclosure, and anyway more dogs about the place would be good, because dog walkers make streets feel watched. You run the audit before you speak. What should you do?
choices: Keep the reversal you can win and give the other part ordinary defense, so one story stands
Say the two responses answer two different arguments of theirs, so the pair can still stand
Add a third answer that shrinks the noise and keep both reversals, so defense can outnumber them
Withdraw the weaker response and grant that the park adds noise, so the stronger one stands alone
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Keep the reversal you can win and give the other part ordinary defense, so one story stands
masteryCheck.hint: One story, not two. Which reversal can you still win?
masteryCheck.explanation: Both answers are about the same outcome, dogs about the neighborhood, and granted together they say your own park removes something you have just called good — which the opponent can simply agree with. The audit says choose: keep one reversal and let the other part take ordinary defense or silence. Keeping both reversals leaves the collision in place, and piling more defense on top does not remove it — counting answers is not the test; answers to two different arguments can collide anyway when they meet on one outcome, and these plainly answer the same one; and granting that your own park adds the noise takes back the reversal you just kept.

teachingSections.heading: Four answers to one chain
teachingSections.body:
Take the skate-park chain and answer it four ways.

“The park will not bring more teenagers — the big regional skate park is two towns over, and small local parks like this sit half empty.” This denies that the action causes the outcome; the chain never starts. That is a NO-LINK. If it succeeds their argument disappears and nothing counts for your side — in the last lesson’s language, defense.

“Teenagers already hang around this neighborhood, skating outside the pharmacy and sitting on the bank steps. A park gathers them into one supervised corner, so the streets see fewer roaming teens, not more.” This does not deny the connection; it reverses the direction — the action lowers the very thing they said it raises. That is a LINK TURN, and it is offense: their own concern now argues for the park. A no-link says the arrow from action to outcome does not exist; a link turn says it points the other way. Different moves with different results, not weaker and stronger versions of one answer.

Now the endpoint, where shrinking comes in two kinds. You can say less of the outcome arrives — “even if the park draws a few more teenagers, it is a dozen skaters on weekend afternoons” — which is really a claim about how strongly the connection works. Or you can say the outcome arrives and matters less than they say: “a dozen skaters on a Saturday afternoon is not the noise and trouble they are describing.” Debaters call the second IMPACT DEFENSE. Both are defense: the outcome stays bad, there is simply less of it or less at stake, and nothing counts for your side.

The endpoint can be reversed too: “more teenagers around is exactly what this neighborhood should want — young people out in the open, visible and known to their neighbors, make a street feel alive instead of empty.” This grants that the outcome happens and reverses its value. That is an IMPACT TURN, offense again, because their predicted outcome is now a reason to vote your way. Shrinking and reversing are different moves: impact defense leaves the outcome bad but smaller; an impact turn makes it good.

teachingSections.heading: When two answers add up against you
teachingSections.body:
Answers can be strong one at a time and still not survive being said together. Run both reversals above and listen to the pair: the park means fewer teenagers around, and more teenagers around would be good. Granted together they say your own plan prevents something you call good, and the opponent can agree with both and take that as the reason to vote against the park. That is the DOUBLE TURN. It is a collision between two claims, not a rule about how many reversals you are allowed.

So the test is about the outcome, not about the labels. Two answers collide when both of them, granted about the SAME outcome — the same measure, the same who or what in the same place, the same stretch of time, the same conditions — add up to a reason against your own side. Note what that does not require: the two claims usually can both be true, and that is exactly why the opponent can agree with both. Run the test in five moves. Name the exact outcome each answer is about. Put both in comparable words. Check whether they are about the same outcome, on all four counts. If they share none of it, they are not candidates for a collision. If they overlap only in part, they are candidates for that part alone: name the part they share and run the last question on it. Then grant them both for the length of the test and ask the question that decides it: granting both, can both stand without making your own side the thing that removes the good, or delivers the harm, that your other answer just named? Matching measures make two claims comparable; only that last question makes the pair self-defeating.

Two things follow, and both matter. Reversals that look like a pair may not be one: “the Saturday market brings fewer weekend loiterers onto the lot than the empty lot draws now” and “the visitors who come to buy from student stalls are good for the school” are about different people, so granting both leaves the opponent nothing. And answers to two different arguments can collide, if they meet on one outcome: thinning teen presence on their noise argument while defending teen presence on their loitering argument is the same self-defeating pair, spread across two flows.

One pairing passes this test rather than dodging it: “it will not happen — and even if it does, it would be good.” The first half is a denial, not a reversal, so it never claims your side removes anything; granting both, your side is not the thing that takes away the good the second half names. Put a reversal in front of the same words and it fails: “the park thins the streets — and even if more teens come, that is good” does claim your side removes the very thing the second half calls good.

teachingSections.heading: What makes a reversal count for you
teachingSections.body:
A reversal counts as offense only when the result it creates would give the judge a reason to prefer your side. The test is what the answer would establish if it were accepted, not whether the judge ends up believing it. Suppose you argue that more teenagers around is good, and the same teenagers would be there whether or not the park is built: you have changed how the outcome is judged and given nobody a reason to choose you. The same holds at the connection — if the teens were never going to roam the streets, proving your park keeps them away wins nothing extra. Ask of any reversal whether the result depends on your side. A reversal that fails that test has not earned the name: it is a claim about something that happens either way, not a turn.

The second duty is this lesson’s own, and it is the same for both reversals. Saying “it flips” is not a reversal: you have to say WHAT reverses, the connection or the endpoint, and WHY the reversed result follows — teens already gather on these streets and a park concentrates them; an evening street with people on it is safer than an empty one. Naming the move tells you what you are trying to accomplish; the reason is what makes it land. Building that into a complete answer, with the because and the therefore, is the refutation lesson’s job.

Two boundaries to keep straight. A reason of your own that does not run through their argument is offense, but it is not a turn: a turn takes their outcome and makes it yours. And an answer aimed at their evidence is an indict from the last lesson, which is defense — going after the evidence becomes a turn only when what you show makes their own argument point your way. The outcome question settles the direction first, every time.

misconception.wrongModel: Two reversals against the same argument are a double turn.
misconception.whyItFails: The number of reversals is not what makes a pair defective. What makes it defective is that the two answers, both granted about the same outcome, add up to a reason against your own side: your plan removes the very thing you have just called good. Two reversals whose outcomes are genuinely different sit together perfectly well, and two answers to two different arguments can collide when they meet on one outcome.
misconception.betterModel: Name the outcome each answer is about, put them in comparable words, check whether those outcomes are the same on all four counts — same measure, same who or what in the same place, same stretch of time, same conditions — and if they overlap only in part, run the last question on the part they share — then grant both and ask whether both can stand without making your own side the thing that removes the good, or delivers the harm, that the other answer just named.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling an answer a turn without saying why the reversed result follows.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: “It actually flips” names a move and gives the judge nothing to believe. A reversal that is only asserted is one the other side can simply deny.
commonMistakes.fix: Say which part reverses, and give the reason it reverses, in one sentence.

commonMistakes.mistake: Denying the connection and calling it a link turn.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: A no-link says the outcome never arrives; a link turn says your side lowers the very thing they said it raises. The first leaves nothing counting for you.
commonMistakes.fix: Ask what is true if the answer succeeds: has the outcome vanished, or has it moved the other way?

commonMistakes.mistake: Reversing an outcome that would arrive either way.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: If the good thing you are now defending happens whether or not your side wins, you have changed how it is judged without giving the judge a reason to choose you.
commonMistakes.fix: Check that the reversed result depends on your side before counting it as offense.

commonMistakes.mistake: Judging a pair of answers by counting reversals.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: Two reversals about genuinely different outcomes sit together perfectly well, and two answers to separate arguments can still collide. Counting is not the test.
commonMistakes.fix: Name the outcome each answer is about, put both in comparable words, and check whether those outcomes are the same on all four counts — same measure, same who or what in the same place, same stretch of time, same conditions — and if they overlap only in part, run the last question on the part they share — then grant both and ask whether they can stand without making your own side remove the good, or deliver the harm, the other just named.

commonMistakes.mistake: Offering a reason of your own and calling it a turn.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: A separate benefit is offense and worth having, but their argument is untouched by it — nothing of theirs has been made to work for you.
commonMistakes.fix: A turn runs through their own outcome. If yours does not, call it what it is.

scaffoldedTry.prompt: The opponent argues: “Moving the library’s story hour to Saturday will bring families onto a street that is already busy with weekend traffic, and more people on foot on a busy street is a hazard.” Your answer: “Families on that pavement on a Saturday morning are what slows the traffic down — drivers go slower on a street where people are walking, and the crossing outside the library is where that matters most.”
scaffoldedTry.frame: Your answer works on ___. If it succeeds, ___. The move is ___.
slots: which part, and what it does to it
the move, in the lesson's words

lesson.title: Explain why your impact wins
lesson.summary: Give the judge a rule for comparing impacts, then apply it to both sides.

content.objective: Give the judge a rule for comparing impacts, argue for that rule, then apply it to both sides.
content.explanation: Weighing explains why one argument matters more than another. Magnitude, probability, timeframe, and reversibility are useful names for common comparison moves — the skill is making the comparison clear, not saying the lens words. Underneath any comparison sits a weighing standard, also called a weighing framework: a rule for deciding, stated so that it could be applied to either side's impact and not only to your own. "A harm that is more likely should count for more" is a standard, because the other side's impact can be tested against it too. "Our harm is huge" is not — there is nothing there for the other side to be measured by. A standard is something you argue for, not something you announce and assume, and the other side can argue for a different one; that disagreement is part of the debate. Putting yours on the table early matters for two reasons: the judge hears it while there are still speeches left in which it can be answered, and the comparison that comes later has something to be measured against instead of two sides asserting that their own impact is bigger. Stating the rule is not the comparison — you still have to show what each impact looks like under it.
content.whyMatters: Judges often believe both sides have some truth. Weighing tells them which truth should decide the round. Without a rule for deciding, the last speeches turn into both sides insisting their own impact is bigger, and the judge falls back on whichever rule they personally happen to prefer. A rule you offered early and defended gives the judge something to apply — and gives the other side time to contest it, which is what makes it fair for the judge to use.
steps: Say what rule you want the judge to decide by, in a form that could be applied to either side.
Give a reason that rule fits this debate, and expect the other side to contest it.
Identify both impacts and show what each one looks like under the rule.
State the comparison the rule produces.

workedExample.prompt: Side A argues an AI-literacy requirement improves student preparedness. Side B argues it costs class time. Here are two ways Side A could run the same comparison across a round.
workedExample.weakAnswer: [Final speech, and nowhere earlier] Decide this on what cannot be undone, because a mistake an institution can repair later is a smaller thing than one a person carries out the door. Lost class time is recoverable — the district adjusts the schedule once — while a student who leaves school unable to check what an AI system tells them carries that gap into work they do not get to redo. Under that rule, preparedness decides.
workedExample.strongAnswer: [First speech] Decide this on what cannot be undone, because a mistake an institution can repair later is a smaller thing than one a person carries out the door. [Final speech] Lost class time is recoverable — the district adjusts the schedule once — while a student who leaves school unable to check what an AI system tells them carries that gap into work they do not get to redo. Under that rule, preparedness decides.
workedExample.whyItWorks: Strip the speech labels and the two versions are word for word the same: the same rule, the same reason for it, and the same comparison. What moves is which speech the rule arrives in. In the strong version it is on the table from the first speech, so the other side still had speeches in which to argue for a different rule, and the judge is applying a rule that was open to challenge. In the weak version the rule appears for the first time beside the conclusion it is meant to justify, when nobody can answer it. The fix for the weak version is not to reorder this speech — it is to have given the rule in an earlier one.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which phrase is weighing?
choices: Our impact is supported by three separate studies
Their impact would be serious if it ever happened
Our impact is bigger and happens sooner
We answered every argument they made today
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Our impact is bigger and happens sooner
guidedQuestion.hint: Weighing compares importance.
guidedQuestion.explanation: This phrase compares magnitude and timeframe. The others describe how well an impact is evidenced, concede a harm without comparing it, or claim coverage — none puts the two impacts side by side.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Aff wins a jobs impact; Neg wins a housing-cost impact. Which response weighs them?
choices: Housing costs are a serious and well-documented burden, and the other side described that harm accurately
Jobs matter more here because lost income reaches more families and cannot be recovered quickly
Our jobs evidence comes from a more recent source than their housing evidence does
Both harms are real, so the judge should treat them as equal and decide on something else
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Jobs matter more here because lost income reaches more families and cannot be recovered quickly
practiceQuestions.hint: Weighing compares the two impacts against each other.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Only this answer compares the two impacts and says why one should matter more. That comparison is weighing, whatever words it uses. The others concede a harm without comparing, compare the evidence rather than the impacts, or refuse to choose at all.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Their impact is huge but very unlikely; yours is smaller but nearly certain. Which comparison resolves that honestly?
choices: The huge impact wins automatically because it is bigger, whatever the chance of it happening
Likelihood is too uncertain to be part of an honest comparison, so set it aside here
Prefer the huge impact, because a harm on that scale would outweigh anything else in the round if it ever actually arrived
Prefer the near-certain impact, because a harm that will almost surely happen should beat one that probably never does
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Prefer the near-certain impact, because a harm that will almost surely happen should beat one that probably never does
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare how likely each impact is, not only its size.
practiceQuestions.explanation: This weighs likelihood against size and tells the judge why likelihood should decide here. A speaker can make this move without ever saying the word probability. The others treat size as automatically decisive, drop likelihood from the comparison, or argue for size without answering how unlikely the harm is.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why weigh arguments?
choices: To show the judge that you covered every argument in the round
To help the judge decide between impacts
To repeat your strongest impact so the judge remembers it
To signal which part of the flow you are speaking on
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: To help the judge decide between impacts
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about decision-making.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Weighing turns competing impacts into a clear decision. Covering arguments, repeating an impact and signposting are all useful, but none of them tells the judge which impact should decide the round.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A round on a town curfew: it might reduce late-night injuries, but it is unlikely to be enforced. Which sentence gives the judge a rule that could be applied to either side's impact?
choices: Late-night injuries are a serious and well-documented harm for teenagers here.
A harm that only lands if a policy is enforced should count for less than one that does not.
Our side has produced more evidence on injuries than the other side has produced.
The curfew is going to reduce injuries by a measurable and meaningful amount.
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: A harm that only lands if a policy is enforced should count for less than one that does not.
practiceQuestions.hint: A rule has to be usable on the other side's impact too, not only on yours.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Only one of these could be turned on either side's impact. The others describe a harm, compare how much evidence each side has, or assert a result — none of them tells the judge how to choose once both harms are real.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which of these is a weighing standard rather than an impact claim?
choices: Thousands of families in the county would lose their only transit access.
Their study on transit ridership was published more than six years ago.
Transit access is the strongest argument our side has made this round.
Harms falling on people with no way to avoid them should count for more.
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Harms falling on people with no way to avoid them should count for more.
practiceQuestions.hint: One of these could be applied to the other side's harm as easily as your own.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A standard is a rule either side's impact can be tested against. The other three name a harm, attack a source, or rank your own arguments — none would help a judge choose between two real harms.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Side A asks the judge to decide on which harm is more likely. Side B thinks reversibility is the better rule. What should Side B do?
choices: Accept Side A's rule, since it was stated first and cannot be changed now.
Ignore rules entirely and simply describe its own impact in more detail.
Argue for reversibility and say why it fits this debate better than likelihood.
Wait until the final speech so Side A has no chance to respond to the rule.
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Argue for reversibility and say why it fits this debate better than likelihood.
practiceQuestions.hint: A standard is argued for, not just announced — and either side can argue for one.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A weighing standard is a claim like any other: the other side can contest it and offer a better one, with a reason. Accepting a rule you disagree with concedes the comparison, ignoring rules leaves the judge to pick their own, and holding a rule back until nobody can answer it makes it weaker, not stronger.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Two speakers both end up arguing that irreversibility should decide the round. Speaker A gave that rule in her first speech and returned to it at the end. Speaker B first raised it in her last thirty seconds. Why is A's version stronger?
choices: A's rule was open to answer while speeches remained; B's arrived too late to contest.
A used more of the standard debate vocabulary than B used in her speeches.
A spent more total speaking time on irreversibility than B managed to spend.
B's rule is the one the judge heard most recently, so it should count for more.
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: A's rule was open to answer while speeches remained; B's arrived too late to contest.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what the other side could do with the rule in each case.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A's rule was on the table while the round was still live, so it could be contested and the final comparison applied a rule that had survived that test. B's rule arrives after the conclusion it is meant to justify, with no time left to answer it. The comparison itself belongs in the last speeches; the rule it runs on should not be new there.

practiceQuestions.prompt: You established early that harms already happening should count for more than harms that might happen later. The other side's harm is a projected budget shortfall in five years; yours is students going without meals now. Which sentence applies the rule you set?
choices: Our impact is far more emotionally compelling than any budget projection is.
A shortfall five years out may never arrive; students are missing meals now.
Budget shortfalls like theirs are almost always exaggerated by the other side.
We should win because we established a weighing rule and the other side did not.
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: A shortfall five years out may never arrive; students are missing meals now.
practiceQuestions.hint: Run both harms through the rule, not only your own.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The correct answer tests both impacts against the standard already established and lets that standard produce the conclusion. The others appeal to emotion, dismiss the other side's harm without using the rule, or treat having a rule as a win by itself — a rule tells the judge how to decide, it does not decide for them.

masteryCheck.prompt: Your harm begins now; theirs arrives years away. Which sentence weighs that difference?
choices: Their harm is years away, which gives everyone involved plenty of time to prepare for it before it lands
Our harm and their harm are both real, so a difference in timing does not change much
Our harm is already starting, so the judge should act on it before their distant harm can even begin
Our harm is happening now and theirs is speculative, so ours is the stronger argument here
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Our harm is already starting, so the judge should act on it before their distant harm can even begin
masteryCheck.hint: Explain why sooner should matter to the decision.
masteryCheck.explanation: This uses the time difference to tell the judge why one impact should decide the round — timeframe weighing, whether or not the word is said. The others assume distance solves the harm, dismiss timing as irrelevant, or stack claims without saying why sooner should decide.

masteryCheck.prompt: A round on rewilding farmland. Side A's harm is species loss that cannot be reversed; Side B's harm is a temporary drop in local farm income. Early on, Side B asked the judge to decide on which harm affects more people day to day, and gave a reason. You speak for Side A, and from your first speech you asked the judge to decide on what cannot be undone. Which final-speech line is strongest?
choices: The number of species that are at stake here is far larger than the number of farms that would be affected by this policy, so we should simply win this round on sheer scale.
You should ignore their rule entirely, judge, because any rule that happens to favour the side that proposed it can never be a fair one to use.
Both harms here are serious ones, so we would ask you to set the standards aside and decide this round on which team has spoken more clearly.
Under everyday reach their harm wins — but in our first speech we asked for a different rule: a harm that ends leaves the county its choices, a permanent one does not.
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Under everyday reach their harm wins — but in our first speech we asked for a different rule: a harm that ends leaves the county its choices, a permanent one does not.
masteryCheck.hint: Ask which line does the most work for a judge who still has to choose between two real harms.
masteryCheck.explanation: This is the hard case: the other side's rule does not favour you. Simply accepting it loses the comparison, and rejecting it because it is inconvenient is not an argument. The strongest line admits what their rule yields, then holds the judge to the rule you put up in your first speech and gives the reason for preferring it — which is what a weighing standard is, a claim either side can contest. The scale option reaches for a rule neither side ever argued for, the ignore-their-rule option rejects a standard for being convenient rather than for being wrong, and the spoke-more-clearly option abandons weighing altogether.

name: Identifying the Problem
description: Separate symptoms from the real business issue.

lesson.title: Find the root business problem
lesson.summary: Choose a recommendation that solves the real issue.

content.objective: State the root problem before proposing a solution.
content.explanation: A symptom is what you notice. The root problem is why it is happening. Strong DECA answers solve the root problem.
content.whyMatters: Judges want business reasoning, not just activity. Identifying the real problem makes your solution more strategic.
steps: Name the symptom.
Ask what causes it.
Choose the problem your solution can affect.

workedExample.prompt: A cafe has many first-time customers but few return.
workedExample.weakAnswer: The problem is not enough customers.
workedExample.strongAnswer: The problem is weak customer retention, not awareness. The solution should focus on loyalty and post-visit engagement.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer separates awareness from retention.

guidedQuestion.prompt: A cafe has many first visits but few repeat visits. What is the root problem?
choices: Customer retention
No awareness
Too many employees
Medical accuracy
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Customer retention
guidedQuestion.hint: Repeat visits are about coming back.
guidedQuestion.explanation: The issue is retaining customers after the first visit.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What is a symptom?
choices: An observable sign of a deeper issue
The final solution
A judge question
A performance score
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: An observable sign of a deeper issue
practiceQuestions.hint: Symptoms are clues.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Symptoms help you infer the root problem.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why state the problem first?
choices: It makes the solution relevant
It replaces the solution
It hides constraints
It lowers confidence
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: It makes the solution relevant
practiceQuestions.hint: Problem before solution.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A clear problem frames the recommendation.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which solution fits retention?
choices: Loyalty program
Random billboard only
Ignore customers
Cut all products
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Loyalty program
practiceQuestions.hint: Retention means repeat behavior.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A loyalty program directly targets repeat visits.

masteryCheck.prompt: If sales are down because checkout is slow, what should you target?
choices: Operations speed
Only brand awareness
Medical terms
Definitions
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Operations speed
masteryCheck.hint: Find the cause.
masteryCheck.explanation: Slow checkout points to operations, not only promotion.

name: Professional Communication
description: Present recommendations with executive clarity and confidence.

lesson.title: Sound like a business advisor
lesson.summary: Use concise structure, business vocabulary, and a confident close.

content.objective: Communicate with a clear opening, numbered points, and professional tone.
content.explanation: Professional communication is not fancy language. It means the judge can trust you because your answer is clear, calm, and business-focused.
content.whyMatters: DECA judges often score delivery and organization alongside the business idea.
steps: Open with the problem and goal.
Give two or three numbered recommendations.
Close with the expected result and how to measure it.

workedExample.prompt: Recommend a promotion plan.
workedExample.weakAnswer: I would do social media and stuff.
workedExample.strongAnswer: I recommend a two-part promotion plan: first, targeted short-form videos for local students; second, a referral offer measured by new customer sign-ups.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer is organized, specific, and measurable.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which opening sounds most professional?
choices: I have a two-part plan to improve repeat visits.
This is easy.
I guess maybe ads.
Whatever works.
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: I have a two-part plan to improve repeat visits.
guidedQuestion.hint: Professional means clear and credible.
guidedQuestion.explanation: This opening frames the goal and structure.

practiceQuestions.prompt: How many recommendation points are usually manageable?
choices: Two or three
Ten
None
Every idea possible
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Two or three
practiceQuestions.hint: Clear beats crowded.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Two or three points allow enough depth without overload.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What should the close include?
choices: Expected result and measurement
A new unrelated idea
An apology only
No conclusion
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Expected result and measurement
practiceQuestions.hint: Business judges like outcomes.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A measurable close shows business reasoning.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which phrase is strongest?
choices: Measured by referral sign-ups
It will be good
People like things
Trust me
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Measured by referral sign-ups
practiceQuestions.hint: Look for measurable business language.
practiceQuestions.explanation: This phrase gives the judge a concrete metric.

masteryCheck.prompt: What does executive clarity mean?
choices: Clear, organized, decision-ready communication
Longer words only
Speaking fast
No structure
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Clear, organized, decision-ready communication
masteryCheck.hint: Think useful to a decision-maker.
masteryCheck.explanation: Executive clarity helps the judge understand and trust the recommendation.

name: Reading Scenarios
description: Quickly identify role, task, audience, and constraints in a DECA prompt.

lesson.title: Read a business scenario
lesson.summary: Find the job to be done before building your recommendation.

content.objective: Extract the role, problem, audience, and constraints from a scenario.
content.explanation: Before solving, pause and mark four things: who you are, who you are speaking to, what problem matters most, and what limits your solution.
content.whyMatters: DECA roleplays reward relevant solutions. If you miss the real scenario, even a polished presentation can score low.
steps: Identify your role.
Identify the decision-maker.
Name the business problem.
List constraints such as budget, time, staff, or brand.

workedExample.prompt: You are a marketing assistant speaking to a store owner about low repeat visits.
workedExample.weakAnswer: I would make more ads.
workedExample.strongAnswer: My role is marketing assistant, the audience is the owner, the problem is low repeat visits, and the solution must improve loyalty without assuming a huge budget.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer reads the situation before solving it.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which detail is the business problem?
choices: Low repeat visits
Marketing assistant
Store owner
The speech room
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Low repeat visits
guidedQuestion.hint: The problem is what needs to improve.
guidedQuestion.explanation: Low repeat visits is the challenge the recommendation must solve.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What should you identify first?
choices: Role and audience
Random slogan
A price discount only
Judge score
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Role and audience
practiceQuestions.hint: Know who you are and who hears the answer.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Role and audience shape tone and recommendation.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why list constraints?
choices: To keep the solution realistic
To avoid solving
To make the answer longer
To skip performance indicators
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: To keep the solution realistic
practiceQuestions.hint: Constraints test feasibility.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Constraints help you recommend something the business can actually do.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which is a constraint?
choices: Limited staff
The word roleplay
A trophy
A speaker rank
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Limited staff
practiceQuestions.hint: Constraints limit implementation.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Limited staff affects what solution is realistic.

masteryCheck.prompt: If the judge is a store owner, how should your tone sound?
choices: Professional and practical
Random and casual
Medical
Courtroom-like
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Professional and practical
masteryCheck.hint: Match the audience.
masteryCheck.explanation: A business owner expects concise, useful recommendations.

name: Healthcare Ethics
description: Make responsible choices using safety, privacy, and respect.

lesson.title: Reason through healthcare ethics
lesson.summary: Use privacy, consent, safety, and fairness to evaluate scenarios.

content.objective: Use ethical principles to choose a safe and respectful response.
content.explanation: Healthcare ethics often involves balancing values like privacy, patient choice, safety, and professional responsibility.
content.whyMatters: HOSA scenarios may test what you do when the easy answer is not the most responsible answer.
steps: Identify the people affected.
Name the ethical issue.
Choose the safest professional action.
Explain why it respects the patient.

workedExample.prompt: A friend asks about a patient's condition.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Tell them if they promise not to share.
workedExample.strongAnswer: I cannot share private patient information. I would direct them to the proper contact process and protect confidentiality.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer protects privacy and gives a professional next step.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which principle is involved when protecting patient information?
choices: Privacy
Marketing
Weighing
Pricing
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Privacy
guidedQuestion.hint: Think about information access.
guidedQuestion.explanation: Patient information should be protected unless sharing is authorized.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What should you do with private patient information?
choices: Share only through appropriate authorized channels
Tell friends
Post it
Guess publicly
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Share only through appropriate authorized channels
practiceQuestions.hint: Privacy rules matter.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Professional ethics requires protecting patient information.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which is an ethical response?
choices: Respect patient dignity
Ignore consent
Embarrass the patient
Skip safety
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Respect patient dignity
practiceQuestions.hint: Ethics centers people.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Respecting dignity supports professional care.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why explain your ethical choice?
choices: To show reasoning and professionalism
To make it longer only
To avoid action
To confuse the judge
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: To show reasoning and professionalism
practiceQuestions.hint: Judges need to see your decision process.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Explaining the principle makes the answer stronger.

masteryCheck.prompt: A scenario involves risk of harm. What principle becomes urgent?
choices: Safety
Advertising
Speaker rank
Budget
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Safety
masteryCheck.hint: Health scenarios prioritize harm reduction.
masteryCheck.explanation: Safety is central when someone could be harmed.

name: Medical Terminology Basics
description: Break clinical words into roots, prefixes, and suffixes.

lesson.title: Decode medical terms
lesson.summary: Use word parts to understand unfamiliar health terms.

content.objective: Break medical terms into word parts and explain them accurately.
content.explanation: Many medical terms are built from prefixes, roots, and suffixes. If you can identify parts, you can understand unfamiliar terms more safely.
content.whyMatters: HOSA events reward accurate health science language. Terminology also helps you communicate clearly with patients and judges.
steps: Find the prefix.
Find the root.
Find the suffix.
Put the meaning together and check context.

workedExample.prompt: Tachycardia
workedExample.weakAnswer: A heart problem.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Tachy means fast and cardia relates to the heart, so tachycardia means a fast heart rate.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer uses word parts and avoids vague guessing.

guidedQuestion.prompt: In tachycardia, what does tachy mean?
choices: Fast
Slow
Lung
Skin
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Fast
guidedQuestion.hint: Think of tachometer: speed.
guidedQuestion.explanation: Tachy means fast.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What does cardi relate to?
choices: Heart
Liver
Bone
Skin
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Heart
practiceQuestions.hint: Cardiology studies the heart.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cardi/cardio refers to the heart.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why use word parts?
choices: To infer meaning safely
To diagnose without context
To avoid communication
To skip definitions
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: To infer meaning safely
practiceQuestions.hint: Word parts are clues, not the whole clinical picture.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Word parts help decode terms while still respecting context.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which is most precise?
choices: Tachycardia means fast heart rate
Tachycardia is bad stuff
Tachycardia is always fatal
Tachycardia means slow breathing
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Tachycardia means fast heart rate
practiceQuestions.hint: Avoid exaggeration.
practiceQuestions.explanation: This answer is accurate and appropriately limited.

masteryCheck.prompt: What does hypo usually mean?
choices: Low or under
High
Heart
Bone
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Low or under
masteryCheck.hint: Hypo means below.
masteryCheck.explanation: Hypo often means low, under, or deficient.

name: Patient Communication
description: Explain health information clearly, respectfully, and safely.

lesson.title: Communicate with patients clearly
lesson.summary: Use empathy, plain language, and confirmation checks.

content.objective: Explain health information in plain language and confirm understanding.
content.explanation: Patient communication combines accuracy and empathy. A strong response avoids jargon, listens to concerns, and checks understanding.
content.whyMatters: In healthcare, communication affects safety. Patients need to understand next steps, risks, and when to ask for help.
steps: Acknowledge the concern.
Explain in plain language.
Give the next step.
Ask a teach-back question.

workedExample.prompt: A patient is nervous about a blood pressure reading.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Your systolic is elevated; just calm down.
workedExample.strongAnswer: I understand this number can feel stressful. Blood pressure can change for many reasons, so we will recheck it and share it with the provider. Can you tell me what step we are taking next?
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer is empathetic, clear, and checks understanding.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which response best uses plain language?
choices: We will recheck your blood pressure and talk with the provider.
Your systolic parameter requires clinical correlation.
Do not worry about it.
This is definitely a diagnosis.
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: We will recheck your blood pressure and talk with the provider.
guidedQuestion.hint: Plain language is accurate and understandable.
guidedQuestion.explanation: This response avoids jargon and gives a safe next step.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What is teach-back?
choices: Asking the patient to explain the next step in their own words
Repeating jargon faster
Ignoring questions
Giving a diagnosis
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Asking the patient to explain the next step in their own words
practiceQuestions.hint: It checks understanding.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Teach-back helps confirm the patient understands.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which tone is best?
choices: Calm and respectful
Dismissive
Sarcastic
Rushed
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Calm and respectful
practiceQuestions.hint: Healthcare communication needs trust.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A calm tone supports professionalism and patient safety.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why avoid jargon?
choices: Patients may not understand it
It is always illegal
It makes answers shorter
It replaces accuracy
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Patients may not understand it
practiceQuestions.hint: Communication is about understanding.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Plain language improves comprehension without sacrificing accuracy.

masteryCheck.prompt: A patient says they are confused. What should you do?
choices: Pause and explain again in simpler language
Move on immediately
Use more abbreviations
Ignore the concern
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Pause and explain again in simpler language
masteryCheck.hint: Respond to the concern.
masteryCheck.explanation: Clear communication includes adapting when the patient is confused.

name: Evidence-Based Reasoning
description: Support claims with examples, reasoning, and responsible evidence.

lesson.title: Support your message with evidence
lesson.summary: Make speeches more credible with support and explanation.

content.objective: Use evidence and reasoning to support a public speaking claim.
content.explanation: Evidence can be an example, data point, expert idea, or personal story. Reasoning explains how the evidence proves the claim.
content.whyMatters: Audiences are more likely to trust a message when they can see why it is true.
steps: State the claim.
Give specific support.
Explain the connection.
Tie it back to the audience.

workedExample.prompt: Claim: practice improves confidence.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Practice is obviously helpful.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Practice improves confidence because repeated rehearsal makes the speech feel familiar. For example, a student who practices the opening five times is less likely to freeze when starting.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer gives reasoning and a concrete example.

guidedQuestion.prompt: What does reasoning do?
choices: Explains how evidence proves the claim
Starts the timer
Removes examples
Changes the topic
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Explains how evidence proves the claim
guidedQuestion.hint: Reasoning is the bridge.
guidedQuestion.explanation: Reasoning connects support to the claim.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which is evidence?
choices: A specific example
A vague feeling only
No support
A transition word
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: A specific example
practiceQuestions.hint: Evidence supports a claim.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Examples can function as evidence when they prove a point.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why explain evidence?
choices: So the audience understands its meaning
To make it confusing
To avoid claims
To skip the conclusion
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: So the audience understands its meaning
practiceQuestions.hint: Do not make listeners infer everything.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Explanation turns evidence into persuasion.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which is strongest?
choices: Practice helps because familiarity reduces fear at the start.
Practice good.
I like practice.
No one needs examples.
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Practice helps because familiarity reduces fear at the start.
practiceQuestions.hint: Look for claim plus why.
practiceQuestions.explanation: This answer gives a reason that supports the claim.

masteryCheck.prompt: A story supports your point only if you also do what?
choices: Explain the connection
Hide the claim
Skip the audience
Use no structure
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Explain the connection
masteryCheck.hint: Evidence needs interpretation.
masteryCheck.explanation: The speaker must show how the story proves the message.

name: Presentation Structure
description: Organize speeches with a clear opening, body, and close.

lesson.title: Structure a clear speech
lesson.summary: Build a speech listeners can follow from start to finish.

content.objective: Use a simple structure: hook, thesis, main points, and close.
content.explanation: Strong speeches feel easy to follow because each part has a job. The opening earns attention, the thesis states the message, the body proves it, and the close makes it memorable.
content.whyMatters: Structure lowers anxiety and helps audiences remember your message.
steps: Start with a hook.
State the thesis.
Organize two or three main points.
Close by returning to the main message.

workedExample.prompt: Speech about why students should learn public speaking.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Public speaking is good and helps people.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Have you ever had a great idea but felt too nervous to say it? Public speaking helps students turn ideas into action. I will show how it builds confidence, clarity, and leadership.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer has a hook, thesis, and preview.

guidedQuestion.prompt: What does a thesis do?
choices: States the main message
Ends the timer
Adds a random example
Replaces the body
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: States the main message
guidedQuestion.hint: The thesis tells the audience what the speech argues.
guidedQuestion.explanation: A thesis gives the speech direction.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What belongs in the opening?
choices: Hook and thesis
Only citations
No topic
A hidden conclusion
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Hook and thesis
practiceQuestions.hint: Openings orient listeners.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The opening should earn attention and state the message.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why use two or three main points?
choices: They are easier to remember
They make the speech endless
They avoid structure
They replace delivery
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: They are easier to remember
practiceQuestions.hint: Audiences remember organized chunks.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A small number of main points improves clarity.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What should a close do?
choices: Return to the main message
Introduce five new topics
Apologize for speaking
Skip the thesis
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Return to the main message
practiceQuestions.hint: The close should land the speech.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A strong close reinforces the central idea.

masteryCheck.prompt: If an audience cannot tell your main point, what is likely missing?
choices: Clear thesis
More volume only
A random joke
A longer timer
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Clear thesis
masteryCheck.hint: The thesis is the main message.
masteryCheck.explanation: A clear thesis helps the audience understand the speech's purpose.
